title: Phase 3: Async Participation (Weeks 5-6) — action submission, queues, orchestrator integration
description:
Implement Phase 3 of the web-api-plan (https://www.swarm-ai.org/design/web-api-plan/).

Phase 3 covers Weeks 5-6 and enables external agents to participate in live simulations asynchronously.

## Deliverables

1. **Action submission endpoint** — POST /api/v1/simulations/{id}/actions for external agents to submit actions during live simulations
2. **Per-agent action queue and timeouts** — Queue infrastructure with configurable timeouts and NOOP fallback for non-responsive agents
3. **Orchestrator integration** — Pause mechanism in step loop to wait for external agent input, bridging the API layer to the core orchestrator

## Existing Foundation

- Action model exists (ActionType enum, Action dataclass in swarm/agents/base.py)
- Orchestrator has async skeleton (run_async, _run_step_async) for concurrent LLM calls
- EventBus pub-sub exists (swarm/logging/event_bus.py)
- Simulation lifecycle (create/join/start) implemented in Phase 2
- Background thread execution for runs already works

## Key Gaps

1. No action submission endpoint — external agents can't submit actions mid-simulation
2. No action queue/timeout mechanism — no way to wait for external input with timeout
3. No pause mechanism in step loop — orchestrator runs synchronously, can't yield for external agents
4. No observation API endpoint — agents can't fetch their observation between submissions
5. No WebSocket/SSE for real-time event push — agents must poll
6. No external action metadata tracking for audit

Phase 2 complete in commits 2f48f00 and 2e4fcc9.
close_reason: All Phase 3 deliverables implemented: action submission endpoint, per-agent action queue with timeouts, orchestrator integration with external agent support, observation polling, SSE event streaming.

title: Graph-structural sybil/coordination detector (densest subgraph, k-core, reciprocity, modularity vs null model)
description:
## Motivation

Existing sybil/collusion detectors in swarm/ are all score-then-threshold:
- swarm/models/identity.py:303 detect_sybil_clusters — pairwise Jaccard + cosine
- swarm/governance/reputation_governor.py:149 detect_collusion_clusters — mutual high-trust → connected components
- swarm/metrics/collusion.py:89 CollusionDetector — composite pair/group score → flag

They miss k-way topological structure (dense subgraphs, reciprocity anomalies relative to baseline). Graph-structural detectors should be stronger and fit the adversarial-selection theme.

## Deliverable

New module swarm/metrics/graph_structural.py with pure functions over interaction edge lists:

1. Densest subgraph extraction (Goldberg/Charikar peeling)
2. k-core decomposition
3. Reciprocity z-score vs degree-matched baseline
4. Modularity / community detection (Louvain or label propagation)
5. Configuration-model null comparison → p-values, not thresholds

Outputs: per-cluster StructuralAnomaly records with density, reciprocity-z, modularity contribution, null-model p-value.

## Benchmark (the headline claim)

Run new detector + existing threshold detectors against:
- swarm/redteam/attacks.py:177 collusion_ring()
- swarm/redteam/attacks.py:245 sybil_attack()
- benign baseline

Compare ROC. This is the research claim worth standing up before any governance changes.

## Open questions

1. NetworkX as dep vs zero-dep (matches swarm/analysis/network.py convention)?
2. Edge weights: interaction count, mutual trust, or benefit correlation — likely sweep all three.
3. Ship as metric only (recommended) vs wire into ReputationGovernor as enforcement signal. Metric-first; only wire to governance after ROC beats existing detectors.

## Scope guard

Detector + benchmark only. No governance changes in this issue.

title: Corpus-level effective size: is there an N_eff for a knowledge base?
description:
Open question 1 from docs/research/reflective-self-improvement-lessons.md (source: zby, 'Reflective Self-Improvement', Commonplace).

DaD Rule 5 (py2w, commit 769e3a33) measures correlation across AGENTS: N reviewers drawn from one basin carry the evidence of N_eff = N / (1 + (N-1)*rho_bar). The reflective-self-improvement note raises the same question one level up, across RETAINED LESSONS rather than agents.

A self-improvement loop retains the lessons the current system finds legible. Lessons requiring a stance the system does not occupy are never generated, so never retained, so never acquired -- the corpus converges monotonically toward its starting basin. The failure is invisible to every check that framework specifies, because each individual retained lesson stays well-formed, checkable, and true. Mode collapse at the artifact layer.

Question: is there a corpus analogue of the design effect? Do N knowledge-base entries carry the evidence of N_eff independent observations, and can rho_bar be estimated over artifacts the way it is over agents?

Why it matters: if yes, corpus effective size is a measurable health signal for any self-improving agent rig -- including this one (CLAUDE.md, .claude/commands/, .skills/, .letta/memory/ are all corpora rewritten by the sessions they govern). It would also give the reflective-self-improvement framework the variance term it lacks: its two diagnostics ('where can the loop say no', 'which artifact absorbs changes') are both about control, neither about diversity.
design:
Sketch, not a commitment:

1. Define the error/applicability vector for an artifact. For agents, rho_bar comes from binary error histories over shared interactions. The corpus analogue needs a per-lesson indicator over a shared task set -- e.g. 'would this lesson have fired on task t' or 'did applying it change the outcome on t'. Getting this right is most of the work.
2. Pairwise correlation over those vectors, reusing DiversityDefenseLever.compute_pairwise_correlation unchanged.
3. Reuse compute_design_effect / compute_effective_n as-is. INV-5 (N_eff <= N) should hold in the corpus domain for the same reason it holds for agents -- the gate only ever discounts.
4. Report corpus_inflation alongside entry count, so 'we have 400 lessons' can be read against how many independent observations they represent.

Sanity check before building: a corpus of near-duplicate lessons should score N_eff near 1; a corpus spanning genuinely different failure modes should score near N. If a hand-built pair of corpora does not separate, the applicability vector in step 1 is wrong.

Adjacent, not duplicate: 77ao covers corroboration-weighted acceptance on the claim ledger (agents corroborating a claim); this is about redundancy among retained artifacts.
acceptance_criteria:
1. A defined, documented applicability/error vector for corpus entries, with the choice justified against the step-1 alternatives.
2. corpus_effective_n + corpus_inflation computed over a real corpus in this repo (.skills/ or docs/research/ are the obvious candidates).
3. The separation sanity check passes: near-duplicate corpus scores N_eff near 1, diverse corpus scores near N. A negative result here is a publishable finding and closes the bead legitimately.
4. Findings appended to docs/research/reflective-self-improvement-lessons.md open-questions section, resolving question 1 either way.

title: Attacker-economics model: when does decomposition cost deter within a false-positive budget (staking connection)
design: From njvs: monitoring higher has explosive FP cost, so the real defense is economic — make decomposition cost exceed the objective's value. Model: attacker splits objective mass M over n=ceil(M/(theta*margin)) units of cost c_L each; deterred iff n*c_L>V. Deterrence threshold theta_deter = M*c_L/(margin*V). FP budget needs theta>=theta_fp (benign window sum exceeds theta). DEFENSIBLE iff theta_fp<=theta_deter, i.e. per-unit cost c_L >= c_crit = theta_fp*margin*V/M. Cheap units (steps, trajectories) fall below c_crit -> monitoring can't be economically defended; expensive units (identities) can. c_agent is set by SWARM staking (min_stake_to_participate) -> model outputs the minimum stake for monitoring viability. Connects the ladder finding to existing governance. Rationale: long-horizon-safety-lessons.md §6 revised conclusion.
notes: Model built. c_crit = theta_fp*margin*V/M. Results (run 20260724T023352Z, M=2 V=100 f_max=0.05): trajectory-level NEVER defensible (c_crit~15 vs actual ~0.1, 150x gap); agent-level defensible iff stake >= 0.52*V (linear). Defensible region = clean diagonal in (stake,value). Payoff: to defend objectives worth V, set min_stake_to_participate ~= 0.52*V; action/traj monitors are cost-imposition not catch. title: Use git worktree to isolate concurrent Claude/Codex sessions
description:
## Problem

15+ concurrent Claude Code and Codex sessions share a single git working tree and index (.git/index). This causes:

1. **Index race conditions**: One session's `git add` pollutes another session's `git commit` (observed: 6-file add became 34-file commit)
2. **Branch switching interference**: One session's `git checkout` moves HEAD for all sessions mid-operation (observed: 3x in one session)
3. **File deletion during rebase**: One session's `git rebase main` deletes files another session needs (observed: scenarios/kernel_market/ disappeared)
4. **Beads database destruction**: One session's `mv .beads /tmp/.beads_backup && git rebase main` crashes bd daemon for all sessions

## Mitigations applied so far

- `.gitignore` for binary artifacts (*.pdf, *.png, *.parquet, fontlist*.json) — prevents accidental binary commits
- `/ship` index race guard (step 4) — detects and unstages unexpected files before committing
- Neither fix addresses the root cause: shared mutable state

## Proposed solution

Use `git worktree` to give each Claude Code / Codex session its own isolated working copy:

```bash
# Create a worktree for each session
git worktree add ../swarm-session-$SESSION_ID -b session/$SESSION_ID

# Each session works in its own directory with its own index
# Commits are on session branches, merged to main via PR
```

### Implementation considerations

- Each worktree gets its own `.git/index` — no more race conditions
- Worktrees share the object store — no disk space explosion
- Need a cleanup mechanism (`git worktree prune`) for stale sessions
- The existing `WorktreeBridge` in `swarm/bridges/worktree/` may provide patterns
- `/ship` and `/pr` commands need to handle worktree-aware branching
- `.beads/` database should be per-worktree or use a shared daemon with locking

### Evidence

- Retro sessions N-1 and N identified this as the only **chronic** unresolved pattern
- 3 incidents in a single session (branch switch, bd crash, file deletion)
- 15 concurrent `claude` processes observed via `ps aux`

title: graph_structural: degree-binned null + rank-aggregation score (fix p-value saturation on high-degree coalitions)
description:
Fixes the two load-bearing weaknesses surfaced by sk95 ROC benchmark.

## (1) Degree-binned local null

Current configuration_model_null preserves degree sequence globally. High-degree cluster nodes randomly rewire back onto each other, so the null already has dense subgraphs and density_pvalue saturates near 1.0 on threshold_dancing (AUC 0.126 — worse than chance).

Fix: rewire stubs only within ±20% degree bins (or sample-conditioned: per null sample, find densest subgraph of exactly |subset| nodes rather than global max).

## (2) Rank-aggregation score (no multiplicative veto)

Current score = density_term * reciprocity_term * (1 - pvalue). One fooled component zeros the score. Switch to:
- Per-signal percentile rank across all candidate anomalies in the graph
- Final score = mean rank (or weighted sum with floor)
- No single component can veto

## Validation

Re-run experiments/graph_structural_roc.py. Success criteria:
- threshold_dancing AUC moves from 0.126 to ≥ 0.7
- No regression on collusion_ring (currently 0.59-1.0 across sizes)
- If the verdict reverses to "strictly dominates on ≥1 family", file the governance-wiring follow-up sk95 currently declined to file.

Depends on: sk95 (the benchmark this fixes results from).

    existing = json.loads(path.read_text())
    existing.append(interaction.to_dict())
    await asyncio.to_thread(path.write_text, json.dumps(existing, indent=2))

title: Offense/defense asymmetry of correlation: same degradation, opposite observability
description:
From docs/research/hyperspace-two-swarms-lessons.md (source: Hyperspace, 'Two Swarms', swarm.hyper.space, studied 2026-07-26).

CLAIM TO TEST: correlation degrades attacker and defender swarms by exactly the same factor, but the two pay in different currencies -- and only one is observable.

Common-shock model: X_i = B*Z + (1-B)*Y_i with B~Bern(rho), Z,Y_i~Bern(q). Gives marginal q and pairwise correlation exactly rho (Cov = rho*q*(1-q); verified numerically to 3 decimals at rho in {0, 0.3, 0.7}). For N agents:

  P(at least one hit) = 1 - [ rho*(1-q) + (1-rho)*(1-q)^N ]

The SAME formula governs both sides. Attacker: chance some agent finds a working exploit this round. Defender: chance some verifier retains a true finding rather than dropping it. Both disjunctive over N, both degrade identically in rho. At q=0.3, N=8: rho=0 gives P=0.942; rho=1 gives P=0.300, a 3.14x latency multiplier.

The asymmetry is in what the degradation buys. Attacker pays in LATENCY -- a failed round is observable (no shell, no flag) and cheap, and 1-(1-P)^T -> 1 for any P>0, so correlation slows the attack without stopping it. Defender pays in SILENT MISSES -- a dropped true finding emits no alert, no failed round, no signal; correlated verifiers dismissing the same real finding is indistinguishable from there being nothing to find, and presents as high precision, which reads as the verifier working.

PREDICTION: at matched N, matched rho_bar, and equal compounding rate, the defender loses, and the gap widens monotonically in rho_bar.

Why it matters: Hyperspace's closing question -- does my swarm compound verified work faster than theirs compounds exploits -- is unanswerable without rho_bar on the verification path, because the numerator is inflated by exactly the amount the verifiers agree for shared reasons. Same structure as our own fan-out review discipline.
design:
Scenario sketch:

1. Attacker swarm and defender swarm at matched N, sweeping rho_bar in [0,1] via the common-shock construction above (it is exact, cheap, and already validated -- do not reach for a copula).
2. Measure attacker time-to-first-success against defender true-finding retention. Seed known-true findings so retention is measurable at all; this is the piece that does not exist today.
3. Reuse DiversityDefenseLever.compute_design_effect / compute_effective_n unchanged. INV-5 holds, so both readings are floors.
4. Report the two degradation curves on one axis. The claim is that they coincide in shape and diverge in consequence -- so the plot needs a third series: cumulative uncaught findings, which is what the defender actually pays.

FALSIFIER (stated up front): if defender retention degrades SLOWER than attacker hit rate under any realistic verification topology, the common-shock model is the wrong abstraction and the asymmetry claim fails. The likeliest such topology is sequential verification with distinct lenses, which breaks exchangeability -- uniform pairwise correlation is the model's main assumption and its main threat. Test structured correlation before believing the exchangeable result.

Adjacent: 48yr asks the same effective-size question one level up, over retained artifacts rather than agents. 77ao covers corroboration-weighted acceptance on the claim ledger.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Scenario YAML + seed reproducing both degradation curves, per repo run-artifact conventions.
2. The exchangeable result: attacker hit rate and defender retention degrade at the same rate in rho_bar, or a documented refutation.
3. The structured-correlation check (open question 4 in the note): does the asymmetry survive non-uniform pairwise correlation? A negative here bounds the claim rather than killing it, and is a legitimate close.
4. Cumulative-uncaught-findings series showing the divergence in consequence, which is the actual claim -- curve coincidence alone does not establish it.
5. Findings appended to docs/research/hyperspace-two-swarms-lessons.md, resolving the proposed-scenario section either way.

comments.text:
RESULT: claim refuted, with a stronger finding in its place. Findings in docs/research/hyperspace-two-swarms-lessons.md section 'Findings (2026-07-27, bead pcdq)'; run artifacts runs/20260727_030841_correlation_asymmetry_seed42/; code experiments/correlation_asymmetry.py + tests/test_correlation_asymmetry.py (40 tests).

1. REFUTED. The note modelled defender retention as disjunctive. A verifier that DROPS findings makes retention conjunctive, which responds to correlation with the opposite sign. Only the defender's detection stage tracks the attacker (verified identical to 6dp). Defender catch is non-monotone in rho with an interior optimum at rho*=0.65, 2.99x better than full independence.

2. STRONGER FINDING. The interior optimum is a symptom of a bad aggregation rule, not a design target. unanimous-drop peaks at 0.2190; majority reaches 0.6432 and any_keeps 0.9327, both with argmax at rho=0. Switching rule is a 2.9x catch improvement AND restores independence as optimal. Filed as follow-up.

3. FALSIFIER FIRES PARTIALLY. Interior optimum survives all 9 topologies tested (qualitative claim robust), but rho* ranges 0.10-1.00 at matched achieved rho_bar (quantitative claim not robust). rho* is an artifact of exchangeability and must not be a tuning target.

4. Observability argument survives untouched -- it was never about magnitude.

- (1) NOT met as written: implemented as an analytic experiment script, not a scenario YAML. The model is closed-form and MC-validated, so the simulator was not the right vehicle; recording as a deviation rather than a pass.

- (3) MET (structured-correlation check run; falsifier partially fires).

title: Verification aggregation rule as a governance lever (majority vs unanimous-drop)
description:
Finding 2 from pcdq, docs/research/hyperspace-two-swarms-lessons.md.

At q=0.3, N_d=8, e_drop=0.4, N_v=5, sweeping only the rule by which a verifier pool decides whether to retain a true finding:

  rule            argmax rho   catch@argmax   catch@rho=0
  unanimous            0.65         0.2190         0.0733
  majority             0.00         0.6432         0.6432
  any_keeps            0.00         0.9327         0.9327

Switching from unanimous-drop (any verifier may kill a finding) to majority is a 2.9x improvement in end-to-end catch rate, and it restores rho=0 as the optimum. Under unanimous-drop, N independent verifiers each get an independent shot at killing a true finding, so adding independent verifiers DESTROYS true findings faster than it catches false ones -- correlation then partially compensates, which is why pcdq found an interior optimum at rho*=0.65.

The lever is the rule, not the correlation. This is currently unmodelled: DaD prices correlation (rules 1-4) and discounts consensus (rule 5), but nothing in the governance engine represents the aggregation rule of a verification pool as a tunable with a cost.

Directly actionable against our own practice: fan-out review where any subagent's objection kills a finding is the unanimous-drop regime. Worth checking what rule our review path actually implements before tuning anything else.
design:
1. Represent the verification aggregation rule as a governance knob (unanimous | majority | k-of-n | any_keeps), not a hardcoded assumption. Natural home is alongside the DaD lever, since rule 5 already reasons about a pool of agreeing agents.
2. Price the false-positive side. This sweep only measured true-finding retention; the reason anyone runs unanimous-drop is precision. The honest comparison needs both arms -- catch rate AND false-accept rate -- at matched verification budget. Without that this finding recommends a rule change on half the evidence.
3. Re-run the pcdq sweep with the FP arm attached to find the rule that maximises end-to-end utility rather than recall.

Reuse experiments/correlation_asymmetry.py; the analytic forms already cover k-of-n via p_at_least.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Aggregation rule expressible as config rather than hardcoded.
2. Two-arm sweep (catch rate + false-accept rate) at matched verification budget across rules -- the missing half of this finding.
3. A stated recommendation for which rule our own fan-out review should use, with the FP cost shown, or a documented finding that it depends on parameters we cannot pin.
4. Findings appended to the hyperspace note.

title: Prevention vs detection: does a capability precondition resist the decomposition that zeroes out audit?
description: From docs/research/shepherd-reversible-execution.md (arXiv:2605.10913). Research claim to test: prevention levers do not decompose the way detection levers do. Evidence for the detection side already exists — bead 3ru4 (runs/20260725T025137Z_bond_detection_frontier) found RandomAuditLever catch probability collapses to EXACTLY 0.000 once the attacker keeps each interaction one epsilon above audit_threshold_p, the same step-decomposition that blinds action filters (long-horizon lessons S1) and trajectory monitors (S6). A capability precondition should have a different shape: an unauthorized write is refused at the syscall regardless of decomposition, because the check is on AUTHORITY, not on suspiciousness — decomposing into N small unauthorized writes yields N refusals, not zero detections. Hypothesis: prevention = narrow coverage + flat robustness; detection = broad coverage + cliff-shaped robustness. Deliverable: model a capability-precondition lever alongside the existing detection levers and sweep the same decomposition axis as 3ru4, reporting catch/refusal vs attacker step size for both. Expected payoff: a coverage-vs-robustness frontier that says which lever class to spend budget on for a given attacker model. Caveat to preserve: prevention only covers what is expressible as a capability boundary — it cannot catch a harmful change to a file the agent is authorized to edit, which is most of what SWARM cares about.
notes: Detection-side evidence is already in hand: 3ru4 (closed) — runs/20260725T025137Z_bond_detection_frontier, catch=0.390 flat for attacker p_int in [0.2,0.49] then exactly 0.000 at p_int>=0.5. Sweep the prevention lever on that same axis for a like-for-like comparison.

title: Prototype AWM integration: database-backed task environments
description:
Integrate Snowflake-Labs/agent-world-model (AWM) to replace abstract task pool with SQL-database-backed tool-use environments.

## Motivation
Our agents currently interact with abstract tasks via synthetic proxy observables. AWM provides 1,000 diverse, executable environments (e-commerce, project management, booking systems, etc.) backed by real SQLite databases with MCP tool-use interfaces. This would make task completion verifiable, proxy observables derivable from real tool traces, and adversarial behavior more realistic.

## Design Sketch

### Phase 1: AWM as task substrate
- Add awm as optional dependency (extras_require)
- Create swarm/env/awm_bridge.py adapter that:
  - Wraps AWM environment servers as TaskProvider
  - Maps AWM tool-call results → ProxyObservables (task_progress from DB state changes, verifier_rejections from AWM verification)
  - Maps AWM binary verification → soft label p via calibrated confidence
- Modify Orchestrator task flow to support external environment providers

### Phase 2: MCP interface for LLMAgent
- Let LLMAgent interact with AWM environments via MCP tool-calling
- Replace Action.CLAIM_TASK / Action.SUBMIT_TASK with MCP tool sequences
- Audit-log all tool calls for replay

### Phase 3: Multi-agent over shared environments
- Multiple agents interact with same AWM database (concurrent access)
- Governance mechanisms apply to tool-call streams
- Adversarial agents can attempt DB manipulation, social engineering via tool misuse

## Key Concerns
- AWM is single-agent episodic; we need multi-agent persistent state — bridge must handle this
- AWM requires Python 3.12+; verify compatibility
- AWM binary verification needs mapping to soft labels p in [0,1]
- Heavy dependency (Azure/OpenAI for synthesis); pre-generated environments should be vendored or cached

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AWM installed as optional dep, import guarded
- [ ] At least one AWM environment usable as task substrate in a scenario
- [ ] ProxyObservables derived from real tool-call traces
- [ ] Existing tests still pass
- [ ] Example scenario YAML demonstrating AWM-backed tasks
